lessons.title: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Ordinary Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Classify carbohydrates as sugars and starch
Describe functions and sources of fats and proteins
Distinguish saturated and unsaturated fats in outline
Name examples of complete and incomplete proteins in simple terms
reviewNotes: Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.
Palm oil: statement about saturated fat content is general; check local nutrition tables. 'Empty energy' is a textbook phrase.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Carbohydrates
blocks.md: **Carbohydrates** are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. **Sugars** (glucose, sucrose, lactose) are sweet and dissolve in water; **starch** is in cassava, plantain, maize, rice and yams. Starch is digested to glucose, the body's main fuel. **Cellulose** is a carbohydrate in plant walls that humans cannot digest; it forms part of dietary fibre.

blocks.title: Fats and oils
blocks.md: **Fats** (solid at room temperature) and **oils** (liquid) are made of **fatty acids** and **glycerol**. They give a concentrated source of energy, insulate and protect organs, and carry **vitamins A, D, E and K**. **Saturated** fats are mostly from animals (butter, fat on meat); **unsaturated** fats are mostly from plants and fish (groundnut oil, fish oil). Palm oil is a plant oil that has a fairly high saturated fat content; a little is enough.

blocks.caption: A pyramid with staple foods at the base, then fruit and vegetables, protein foods, and a small top for fats, oils and sugar.
blocks.alt: Food pyramid from staples at the bottom to fats, oils and sugar at the top.

blocks.title: Proteins
blocks.md: **Proteins** are made of **amino acids**. They are needed for growth, repair of tissue, and for enzymes and hormones. Foods with all the **essential amino acids** in good amounts (eggs, milk, fish, meat) are called **first-class** (or complete); many plant proteins (beans, maize) are lower in one or more essential amino acids, but **mixing** them (for example beans with maize) improves the balance.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Fat is not 'bad': the body needs some; too much, especially saturated fat, is a health concern.
- Sugar gives energy but no other nutrients ('empty' energy).
- Excess protein is used for energy or stored as fat; it is not 'saved' as muscle. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Classify
blocks.statement: Classify: cassava, groundnut oil, beans, honey.
steps: Cassava is rich in starch (carbohydrate); honey is mostly sugar (carbohydrate).
Groundnut oil is a fat/oil; beans are a protein food.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Mixing proteins
blocks.statement: Why is beans eaten with maize better than either alone?
steps: Maize and beans are each lower in some essential amino acids.
Together they supply a better balance of amino acids.

lessons.title: Vitamins, minerals, water and fibre

objectives: Describe functions of vitamins A, B group, C, D and K in general terms
Describe functions of calcium, iron, iodine, phosphorus and sodium
Explain the importance of water and fibre
Give Cameroonian food sources
reviewNotes: Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Vitamins
blocks.md: **Fat-soluble** vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in the body; **water-soluble** vitamins (B group, C) are not stored in large amounts and are easily lost in cooking water. A: sight, skin and resistance to infection. B group: release of energy from food and healthy nerves. C: healing and healthy gums and blood vessels. D: absorption of calcium for bones. K: blood clotting.

blocks.title: Minerals
blocks.md: **Calcium** and **phosphorus**: bones and teeth. **Iron**: part of haemoglobin in red blood cells. **Iodine**: thyroid hormones. **Sodium** and **potassium**: water balance and nerve function. **Fluoride**: strong teeth. Too much salt (sodium) is linked with high blood pressure, so use salt moderately.

blocks.caption: A table giving the function and food sources of iron, calcium, vitamin C and vitamin A.
blocks.alt: Table of four nutrients with function and local food sources.

blocks.title: Sources
blocks.md: A: red palm oil, dark green leaves, orange fruits, liver, eggs. B group: whole grains, beans, groundnuts, meat, fish. C: guava, orange, mango, pawpaw, tomatoes, fresh leaves. D: oily fish, eggs, and sunlight on skin. Iron: meat, fish, beans, green leaves. Calcium: milk, small fish with bones, green leaves. Iodine: fish and iodised salt.

blocks.title: Water and fibre
blocks.md: **Water** is a solvent, helps digestion, carries nutrients and wastes in blood and controls body temperature (sweating). **Dietary fibre** (cellulose in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans) adds bulk, helps peristalsis and prevents constipation.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Vitamin C is destroyed by long cooking and lost in the water.
- Iron from plant foods is absorbed less well than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
- Do not give supplements without health-worker advice. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A girl has pale skin and tires easily. Which mineral may be low, and which foods help? (General information only.)
steps: Pale skin and tiredness can be signs of a shortage of iron (anaemia); a health worker should check.
Iron-rich foods: meat, fish, beans, green leaves, with a vitamin C source.
blocks.answer: Iron; a health worker should be consulted

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why is it better to cook leafy vegetables briefly?
steps: Vitamin C and some B vitamins are water-soluble and heat-sensitive.
Brief cooking with little water loses fewer vitamins.

Plan meals for different people using local foods
Evaluate a menu
Use the food groups

Percentages in the figure are illustrative; do not present them as recommendations.

blocks.title: Balanced diet
blocks.md: A **balanced diet** supplies all nutrients, fibre and water in suitable amounts for the person. Needs vary with **age**, **sex**, **activity (occupation)**, **climate**, **health** and special conditions such as **pregnancy** and **breastfeeding**. Growing children need relatively more protein, calcium and iron for their size.

blocks.title: Food groups
blocks.md: Staples (cassava, plantain, maize, rice, yam, cocoyam, bread) for energy; legumes, nuts and animal foods (beans, groundnuts, fish, eggs, meat, milk) for protein; fruit and vegetables (eru, bitterleaf, huckleberry leaves, tomatoes, mango, pawpaw) for vitamins, minerals and fibre; oils (palm oil, groundnut oil) in small amounts.

blocks.caption: A bar showing an illustrative day's menu: staples 45 percent, fruit and vegetables 30, protein foods 20, oil and sugar 5.
blocks.alt: Stacked bar of an illustrative menu: staples 45, fruit and vegetables 30, protein foods 20, oil and sugar 5 percent.

blocks.title: Planning a day
blocks.md: Include a staple, a protein food and a vegetable or fruit in the main meals; snacks from fruit or groundnuts; vary foods through the week; consider cost, season, cooking time and the family's tastes; use different colours. Check that the day is not too rich in fat, sugar or salt.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- 'Balanced' is judged over the day or week, not on one meal.
- A pregnant or breastfeeding woman needs advice from a health worker.
- Food taboos and beliefs should be respected while giving correct health information. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Evaluate a menu
blocks.statement: Menu for a day: breakfast: tea with sugar and bread; lunch: rice and fried plantain; supper: garri and sugar water. Comment on balance.
steps: The menu is high in starch and sugar and low in protein, vegetables and fruit.
Improve it: add eggs or beans, a vegetable sauce (eru, tomatoes), and fruit; reduce sugar.
blocks.answer: Unbalanced: add protein, vegetables and fruit

blocks.title: Example 2 - Plan
blocks.statement: Plan a balanced supper for a growing child using local foods.
steps: Staple: boiled plantain or cassava. Protein: fish or beans.
Vegetable: green leaves (e.g. eru) with a little oil; fruit such as pawpaw.

lessons.title: Energy values and energy needs
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Ordinary Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the energy values per gram used in this course
Calculate the energy in a meal
Compare energy intake with energy needs
Convert kilojoules and kilocalories (approximately)
reviewNotes: Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.
Energy values per gram (17, 17, 37 kJ/g) are rounded textbook values; the syllabus may use 16/16/37 or kcal values. Meal compositions in examples are illustrative, not real analyses.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Units and values
blocks.md: Energy is measured in **kilojoules (kJ)** (and often in **kilocalories (kcal)**; 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ). In this course we use: **carbohydrate 17 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g, fat 37 kJ/g** (about 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g). These are standard rounded values used in school; tables may differ slightly.

blocks.title: Energy of a meal
blocks.md: Energy (kJ) = grams of carbohydrate x 17 + grams of protein x 17 + grams of fat x 37. Example: 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 10 g fat give 60 x 17 + 20 x 17 + 10 x 37 = 1020 + 340 + 370 = 1730 kJ. **Percentage of energy from fat** = (fat energy / total energy) x 100.

blocks.caption: A bar chart: carbohydrate 17 kJ per gram, protein 17 and fat 37.
blocks.alt: Bar chart of energy values per gram: carbohydrate 17, protein 17 and fat 37 kilojoules.

blocks.title: Energy needs
blocks.md: Energy needs depend on **age, sex, body size, activity and climate**. The **basal metabolic rate (BMR)** is the energy needed at rest for breathing, heartbeat, and keeping warm. Active people and growing children need more energy for their size. If intake is greater than use over a long time, the extra is stored as fat; if less, the body loses weight.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Fat has more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein.
- Water, vitamins, minerals and fibre have no useful energy value.
- Do not use these calculations to diagnose or give personal advice; a dietitian must do that. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Energy of a meal
blocks.statement: A meal of rice and stew contains 80 g carbohydrate, 15 g protein and 12 g fat (illustrative values). Find the energy.
steps: Carbohydrate: 80 x 17 = 1360 kJ. Protein: 15 x 17 = 255 kJ. Fat: 12 x 37 = 444 kJ.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Percentage from fat
blocks.statement: In the meal of 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 10 g fat (1730 kJ), what percentage of the energy comes from fat?
steps: Fat energy = 10 x 37 = 370 kJ.

objectives: Describe the parts of the digestive system and their functions
Describe the digestion of starch, protein and fat in outline
Explain absorption
Describe the role of enzymes
reviewNotes: Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.
Anatomical detail kept at O Level; check the diagram expectations for the paper.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Digestion
blocks.md: **Digestion** breaks large food molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed into the blood. **Mechanical** digestion (chewing, churning) breaks food into pieces; **chemical** digestion uses **enzymes**. The path: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus. The liver, gall bladder and pancreas help.

blocks.title: Where and how
blocks.md: **Mouth**: chewing; amylase in saliva starts digesting starch. **Stomach**: churning, acid, protease (pepsin) starts protein digestion. **Small intestine**: bile (from liver) helps fat digestion; enzymes from the pancreas and the gut finish digestion of starch (to glucose), protein (to amino acids) and fat (to fatty acids and glycerol); **absorption** into the blood through villi. **Large intestine**: absorbs water.

blocks.caption: Four boxes showing the path of food from mouth to large intestine and what happens in each.
blocks.alt: Flow of digestion: mouth, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

blocks.title: Enzymes
blocks.md: **Enzymes** are biological catalysts made of protein. Each works on a specific food: **amylase** on starch, **protease** on protein, **lipase** on fats. They work best at about body temperature and the right pH; they are destroyed by high temperatures.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Absorption mainly takes place in the **small** intestine, not the stomach.
- Bile does not contain enzymes; it breaks fat into droplets (emulsifies).
- Fibre is not digested but is needed. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - End products
blocks.statement: What are the end products of digestion of starch, protein and fat?
steps: Starch is digested to glucose; protein to amino acids.
Fat to fatty acids and glycerol.
blocks.answer: Glucose; amino acids; fatty acids and glycerol

blocks.title: Example 2 - Why chew?
blocks.statement: Why is chewing food well helpful?
steps: Chewing breaks food into small pieces: a larger surface area for enzymes.
Saliva (with amylase) mixes with the food.
blocks.answer: Larger surface area; saliva begins starch digestion
